sanskrit: यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत ।
translit: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata
hindi: हे भारत! जब-जब धर्म की हानि होती है और अधर्म बढ़ने लगता है, तब-तब मैं स्वयं को प्रकट करता हूँ।
english: Whenever goodness declines and wrongdoing rises, O Bharata, then I bring myself forth into the world.
deeper: This is one of the most loved promises in the Gita: goodness is never abandoned. In the next verse (4.8), Krishna says he comes, age after age, to protect the good, to end evil, and to set dharma right again. Stories of Rama, Narasimha and Krishna himself are seen as this promise kept.
Dharma here doesn’t just mean religion. It means what is right, fair, true and kind — the order that keeps life healthy.

There is also an inner meaning: whenever wrong starts rising inside our own heart — a lie, jealousy, cruelty — the divine voice of conscience wakes up too. And when we stand up for what is right, we become small instruments of that same divine promise.
background: At the start of Chapter 4, Krishna says that he taught this ancient yoga long ago to Vivasvan, the Sun god, who taught it to Manu, who taught it to King Ikshvaku — but over time it was lost (4.1–3).

Arjuna is puzzled: “You were born recently, and Vivasvan lived ages ago. How could you have taught him?” (4.4). Krishna replies that both of them have had many births — he remembers all of his, Arjuna does not (4.5). Though he is unborn and eternal, he appears by his own power (4.6). Then he tells Arjuna when and why he comes.
lessons: Never lose hope in dark times.
Goodness always finds its way back.
Stand up for what is right.
When you protect someone weaker, you join God’s work.
That uneasy feeling before doing wrong is your conscience speaking.
Truth may feel alone at first, but it is never truly alone.
It is lived in small daily choices, not just in temples.
examples: A child was being teased again and again. Zoya stood by him and told the teacher. The wrong was stopped.
A friend asked Manan to help him cheat in the exam. Manan politely refused — he chose honesty.
Seeing an injured puppy on the road, Ansh and his mother took it to the vet.
The children of the colony planted 20 saplings in the park and took turns looking after them every day.
Arya found a wallet on the road and returned it to its owner — even though nobody had seen her pick it up.
A friend said, “Just lie to the teacher.” A voice inside Riya said, “This is wrong.” She listened to that voice.
Someone at home was ill and everyone was sad. Grandma said, “However dark the night, morning always comes.” And truly, everything got better.
At lunch, nobody let one boy sit with them. Samar picked up his tiffin and went to sit beside him.

story.title: Prahlad and Lord Narasimha
paras: The demon king Hiranyakashipu had a boon: he could not be killed by man or beast, by day or by night, inside a house or outside it. Full of pride, he declared, “I am God!”

But his young son Prahlad chanted “Narayana, Narayana” all the time. His father tried everything to frighten him — had him thrown from a cliff, made him sit in a fire on his aunt Holika’s lap — but every time, Prahlad was saved.
At last, in a rage, Hiranyakashipu pointed at a pillar. “Where is your God? Is he in this pillar?” Prahlad calmly replied, “Yes, Father. He is everywhere.”
Hiranyakashipu struck the pillar — and it burst open! Out came Lord Narasimha, half man and half lion. At dusk, on the doorstep, he ended the tyrant and lovingly lifted Prahlad into his lap.
story.moral: Lesson: When wrongdoing grows, God surely protects the good. Stand firm on the side of truth.

quiz.q: According to Krishna, when does he appear?
o: When goodness declines and wrongdoing rises
quiz.x: “Yadā yadā hi dharmasya glāniḥ” — whenever dharma declines.

quiz.q: What form did God take to protect Prahlad?
quiz.x: Lord Narasimha — half man, half lion — came out of the pillar.
Glāniḥ means a decline or weakening.

quiz.q: What did Arjuna ask just before this teaching?
o: You were born later — how did you teach the Sun god?
quiz.x: In 4.4 Arjuna asked this, and verses 4.5–4.8 are Krishna’s answer.

reel.hook: Does goodness always win? Krishna made a promise.
reel.lesson: When wrong rises, stand up for what is right.
reel.caption:
A promise from Krishna 🪔
Goodness is never left alone.
